narrative:
The model estimated a 51.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is just over a coin-flip risk, not a certainty, but it was enough for your law school application to be denied under the admission process that uses this prediction.

The strongest reason was your LSAT score. At 23, it is well below the average of about 37 for students who were accepted, and it was the single most influential factor pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The second most important factor was your family income bracket. Being from a lower-middle-income family counted in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing, but its influence was smaller than the LSAT disadvantage. The third most important factor was your first-year class-rank decile. At 4, you were below the accepted-student average of about 6, and this factor also worked in your favor toward passing. Even so, the LSAT signal outweighed these supportive factors, leaving the estimated failure risk at 51.0%.

Your gender and race did not drive this decision. The most useful next step is to improve your LSAT profile through structured preparation and, if feasible, a retake, because that was the dominant factor. You should also meet with admissions to discuss how a stronger LSAT and any additional academic evidence could change your chances; at 51.0%, even a modest improvement could move the prediction below the denial threshold.
